speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My speech will set the context and put forth recommendations for the Ministry’s consideration.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Thereafter, hon Member Nadia Abdul Samdin will build on further.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, on recognising the role of MDWs in caregiving.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore’s society structure has changed as we progress.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And with an ageing population, the demand for care increases.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The average resident household size in 2020 was 3.22, whereas it was 4.25 in 1990.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: That is equivalent to one less person in the family to share anything within a 20-year period.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Thirdly, more members of a household are working.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Taken together, the need for care is increasing but the capacity of families to care for their loved ones is diminishing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, ensuring availability and accessibility to caregivers and caregiving services become increasingly important.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In keeping pace with the changing social structure in Singapore, the Government must, of course, be recognised for making tremendous effort to support Singaporean families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One, care capacity in the form of day care centres and care institutions increased.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For instance, the number of home care and day care places increased to 10,300 and 9,000 respectively in 2019.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Infant care centres and childcare centres increased 30% and 11% respectively within the same period.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, certified educators in the early childhood sector grew by 30% between 2016 and 2020.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Two, a range of childcare and eldercare subsidies and assistance schemes was introduced over the years to enhance affordability, including the Seniors’ Mobility and Enabling Fund and the Home Caregiving Grant to support caregivers who gave up their jobs to care for their loved ones and low- or no-income care recipients.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, the role of migrant domestic workers remains integral to how Singaporean families choose to provide care or supplement caregiving for their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is equivalent to having "every fifth Singaporean household (hiring) a maid", and I am quoting from CNA.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am also sure that we have heard of heartwarming stories of how MDWs grew with families and became an integral household member over time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There are challenges faced by families hiring MDWs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, there have been cases of MDWs being abused or mistreated by their employers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Such egregious cases must be made known and properly dealt with by the law.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: MOM and several non-government organisations’ efforts in ensuring proper and fair treatment of MDWs should be recognised.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But most Singaporean families who hire MDWs are decent employers who need care support at home and who do take care of their MDWs, pay on time and try their best to do good on their own.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In my many conversations with residents, I have learnt of the struggles that some of these families face with their MDWs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Following my Parliamentary Questions in September and October 2021’s Sittings, more Singaporeans from within and outside of my constituency wrote to me to share their own experiences.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: From the stories they shared, the challenges they face can be broadly categorised into three types: number one, escalating salary expectations; number two, disputes, specifically allegations of abuse; and number three, demand for transfer "or else".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These challenges had been fomenting pre-COVID but the challenging situation "boiled over" when the supply of MDWs was curbed by travel restrictions during the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: When the inflow of MDWs was controlled to a trickle, families desperate for help turned to those available for transfers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, the supply fell but demand continued to rise, resulting in a price surge.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the Minister for Manpower’s written reply to my Parliamentary Question in September this year, I note that the monthly salary increased from $570 to $590 for new MDWs and $610 to $630 for transfer MDWs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: That translates to about 3.2% to 3.5%, and that is from end 2019 to end 2020.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And in the more recent report which was published yesterday, I think this has gone up to $660 for transfer MDWs just earlier this year.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, I was also told that in a bid to secure helpers urgently, some salary offers went up to as high as more than $1,000 per month on top of paying for food, accommodation and medical expenses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: The image on-screen is small, but this is an example.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Such offers were publicised in Facebook groups such as "Singapore transfer helpers (maids) direct hire".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: One Facebook user called "Minyu", who commented on my page, shared that some agents poach MDWs by offering higher salaries so that the agents can benefit from the additional agent fee.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: This, if true, will undoubtedly exacerbate the situation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Families stunned by such requests have little option – they could not just find a replacement easily especially during the pandemic period.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Many of such families dare not ask the MDWs to honour the contracts and stay on because their loved ones are literally in the hands of the MDW.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Hence, they either offer a higher salary or consent to the transfer.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: The latter obviously leaves families with real care needs in the lurch.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Such phenomenon would also come across as favouring the high earners.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: A young working mother of two called "AK" in short, shared with me in an email that her helper accused her family of providing insufficient food and rest and demanded a transfer.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Thankfully, "AK" had CCTV footages to prove that the allegations were untrue.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Several other Singaporeans shared their unpleasant experiences with me via social media and through conversations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Upon receiving complaints of possible abuse, MOM would have to investigate and the process can take months.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: During this time, the families face challenges hiring replacements.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: And even if the allegations were eventually found to be baseless, the MDWs often faced no legal consequence and were sent back to their home countries, at worst.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Innocent families that had endured the ordeal are then left to pick up the pieces on their own.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Again, it must be recognised that there are egregious cases of real abuse and these must be dealt with by the law.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: But false allegations without real consequences seem unfair too.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: As such, a number of Singaporean employers wrote to me to express their desire for fairer treatment and called for more help.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: This mitigates the challenging situation to some extent, but some underlying issues remain to be solved.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: First, on improving access for middle-income or "sandwiched" families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Second, to introduce consequences for errant irresponsible MDWs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: So, the second one is to ensure completeness of individual MDWs' employment history so that it is usable.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: A Singaporean employer by the name "Han" who hired a MDW to care for her grandparents shared her experiences over email.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: She showed me screenshots of the MDW's history of several employment but the column for reason of cancellation was entirely blank.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: She asked how could one objectively assess prospective MDWs?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Therefore, could MOM consider requiring employment agencies (EAs) to fill in the reason for cancellation or allow employers to do so directly?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Many families also do not know of the existence of such records and it would be very useful if more publicity can be done.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Third, to encourage matching to be taken more seriously, could MOM consider imposing a cap on the number of transfers initiated by the MDW in a year?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Exceeding that cap with no valid reason and proof would then require the MDW to return to their home country.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Presently, I am aware that employers who repeatedly request for transfers in a short period of time face restrictions in hiring MDWs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: So, it would seem fair to ensure all parties involved to take the contract seriously.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Fourth, could there be more stringent checks or restrictions on MDWs with a poor performance record when re-entering Singapore for new jobs?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: So, the fifth recommendation is that I learnt from MOM's response to my Parliamentary Question last month that the Ministry is working to encourage EAs to take greater ownership of matching outcomes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: If so, could the MOM consider allowing the matching of MDWs be done by local EAs only, that is, to disallow private bartering via social media platforms which are unregulated?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: However, I understand that there are concerns about whether this will give EAs too much power and risk high agency fees.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Perhaps, MOM could pay more attention to this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: The sixth and last recommendation is that many Singaporean families who need MDWs for care needs are crying for greater support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Some are busy trying to make ends meet and some are just not savvy with the systems.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Thus, could MOM consider establishing neutral advisory channel or platform offering these families information and consultations?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: In ensuring a successful relationship between the employer family and the MDW will require genuine efforts and mutual respect from both parties.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Hence, I hope with the challenges addressed, families will feel more supported and better able to focus on their work and pursue a happier life.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, care support is of utmost concern not just for our elders but for the adult children who bear the responsibility to look after their own children and their aged parents.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It has been said in this Chamber that the true costs of caregiving affects certain groups disproportionately.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During the closing session of the conversations on Singapore women's development, the Prime Minister acknowledged that women often tend to have additional caregiving responsibilities for both young and old and that more can be done to support them emotionally and financially.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Dependence on such unpaid family caregivers who are usually women is not longer tenable.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the late 1970s, the foreign maid scheme was launched to enable families to employ MDWs and support women's participation in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In May this year, it was announced that all new entry approvals for work pass holders from countries with higher risk of COVID-19 will be temporarily halted, including Indonesia, Philippines and Myanmar, all three of which provide the bulk of Singapore's MDWs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of us would have had residents appealed to us to allow MDWs to secure entry approvals to care for both young and old in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With dual income households now forming more than half of all married couples as of 2020, an MDW is often considered an important of fulfilling caregiving needs for families from various income backgrounds.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Aside from MDWs, what caregiving solutions are available for seniors?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: AIC has developed the network of community care services which fall under three broad themes: homecare, daycare and stay-in care.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And despite the pandemic, some reports have suggested that the demand for MDWs remains steady, if not, increased, even as costs trended upwards.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: MDWs continue to be important as part of our caregiving landscape for a few key reasons.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, seniors have complex needs and applying for different segregated services can be more expensive and inconvenient.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Cheng San-Seletar, I am very grateful for community befrienders who often step in to accompany seniors, who are fall risks to their hospital appointments.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the other hand, home personal care costs cost approximately $20 per hour prior to means test subsidies and referrals from hospitals or polyclinics are often required.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With higher collective costs and sometimes incomplete combinations of services, hiring an MDW is often a coherent solution.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, our seniors tend to price independence and have preferences against institutionalised care.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The perceived loss of independence in a nursing home is something they are concerned about and so children hire MDW as this support is compatible with their filial duty to meet their parents' desires to age-in-place without compromising on safety.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One possible solution is the model recently announced by HDB, MOH and MND: the Community Care Apartments to encourage independent living.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And I am very much looking forward to see how care can be better aggregated so our seniors live with dignity in their golden years.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, prior to the pandemic, families often turned to MDWs as a more timely solution due to unfamiliarity with existing schemes and the limited time in finding suitable caregiving options.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some have also raised concerns about the waiting list for subsidised elder sitting services and nursing homes and looking for suitable step-down care services causes stress for families.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many also find it risky to wait and see if their loved ones qualify for a subsidised space or not.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Closer attention should be paid to the matching and training of our MDWs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are stories of MDWs experiencing burnout when expectations of their jobs are mismatched with the tasks required.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A study conducted by AWARE and HOME shared this sentiment, pointing to the lack of information provided by employers and verification by employment agencies.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We could look at establishing a more thorough needs assessment, which can be verified by employment agencies through submitted health records.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Should that be a mismatch of skills and job requirements, employers can then apply for the caregivers' training grant to upskill the MDW.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another proposal would be expanding the homecare giving grant (HCG).

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Qualifying for the grant requires means testing and assessment of the care recipient's ability to carry out activities of daily living or ADL.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These measures ensure that the ones with the most needs receive the grant but it leaves a gap where vulnerable groups can fall into.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, a dual income couple with an elderly mother and two young children may find themselves needing an MDW but they may fail to qualify for the HCG because their elderly mother only requires assistance to perform two ADLs, despite having other chronic health issues.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even though hiring an MDW may be the least expensive option, this sandwiched class of families will be paying the full price.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We could explore a points-based system where the number of ADLs that require assistance in household per capita, a monthly income can be tiered.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In closing, I wish to acknowledge and highlight the challenges faced by many Singaporeans during this pandemic in employing MDWs to support caregiving needs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some have described being at their wits end, finishing up annual leave to race to their loved ones’ side.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One resident shared that while waiting for the entry approval of an MDW to be approved, she would take turns to care for her elderly mother who was a fall risk, with her brother.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The daughter felt a deep sense of filial piety and did not insist.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, when her brother and his family was on Quarantine Order, the 14 days back then which ensued were a nightmare for her as she struggled to balance work and caregiving, and even thought about quitting her job.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I know many families have faced this dilemma too and hope we can look ahead to ensure that our caregiving needs are met, women are allowed to participate actively in the workforce and we also support our MDWs to be more equipped and better prepared for the roles they take on in our families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In my response, I will address the following points: one, MDWs' role in the caregiving landscape in Singapore; and two, measures to support employers in hiring and managing domestic helpers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I share Members' views that MDWs continue to be important to support households with caregiving needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Over the years, the Government has dedicated efforts to improve accessibility, affordability and quality of care options overall.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These include expanding the capacity of long-term care services for seniors and persons with disabilities, childcare and afterschool care centres for children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MND, MOH and HDB have also launched the first assisted living flats in February this year, which integrate senior-friendly design features with care services that can be scaled according to the care needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This enables seniors to live independently while meeting their current and future care needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To improve the affordability of care, various subsidy schemes have been put in for residential, day and homecare services, respite care services, childcare and infant care services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Families may apply for the means-tested Home Caregiving Grant, which can be used flexibly for different caregiving expenses, such as hiring of MDWs to care for an individual with permanent moderate disability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MOH is reviewing the Home Caregiving Grant to provide more help for targeted groups.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: With the increasing complexity of care provision, it is important for MDWs to be trained in essential skills for caregiving.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Employers may enrol their MDWs for various training courses to empower them to provide higher-quality care.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Today, there are 200 training courses provided by 50 training providers that are available for employers to send their domestic helpers to.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: They may tap on the Caregivers Training Grant to offset training costs for the care of elderly or disabled loved ones.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some employers have managed to do without MDWs by tapping on institutional care options or engaging companies under the Household Services Scheme to meet their household needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: However, for many employers, the options I have mentioned may not fully meet their needs and MDWs remain important to them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, employers have been impacted by the limited supply of MDWs to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Amidst the shortage of MDWs, some employers face requests by their MDWs for higher wages or a transfer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I understand the difficulties an employer goes through if an MDW seeks a transfer before the end of the contract.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As I mentioned in the House yesterday, the local and regional COVID-19 situation continues to stabilise and we have begun to grant more entry approvals for MDWs to come to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The current MDW supply crunch is expected to improve in the coming months.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In the longer term, MOM will diversify the countries from which MDWs are hired.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: However, we must recognise that there will continue to be competition for MDWs, not just locally but also from countries in the region.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Besides reasonable remuneration to attract MDWs to work in Singapore, there is also a need to position Singapore as an attractive workplace destination for MDWs, to ensure resilience in our MDW supply.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Other than the measures to enable a steady stream of MDWs for Singapore, it is equally important to ensure that employers are matched with MDWs who best meet their needs, as well as provide support to employers and MDWs to foster good employment relationships.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Members have suggested that matching be done only by local employment agencies (EAs) and to disallow direct hiring of MDWs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For the remaining employers who prefer to hire their MDWs directly to avoid incurring additional costs of engaging an EA, disallowing them to self-help would inadvertently increase their costs of hiring MDWs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Instead of placing a cap on the maximum number of transfers for an MDW, MOM has adopted the approach of making information more transparent so that employers can make informed decisions when hiring MDWs, including those who have had frequent transfers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Employers may access information relating to prospective MDWs’ work experiences and the types and sizes of households that they have worked in before.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Employers can also view the length of each past employment and the reasons why these MDWs left their past employers, including information on the party that initiated the discontinuation of employment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We started collecting the reasons from employers for the cancellation of MDW's Work Permits since September last year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: With time, the information in the MDW employment history will become more comprehensive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The employer reference channel also allows prospective employers to contact the former employers of the MDWs they are looking to hire for reference checks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MOM will look into how we can raise awareness of these existing measures amongst employers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Other than improving matching outcomes, MOM has also put in place measures to support employers and MDWs during the course of employment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: It is not uncommon for there to be differences in expectations in a working relationship, especially at the initial stage when both parties are adjusting, be it to a new environment or having a new person living in your home.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Most misunderstandings between MDWs and their employers are resolved amicably.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: However, like Members alluded to, there are instances where both parties are unable to resolve the disputes on their own.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For such cases, help can be sought from the employment agencies and via dispute resolution services offered by professionals through the Foreign Domestic Worker Association for Social Support and Training (FAST) and Centre for Domestic Employees (CDE).

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MOM officers work with the Police to investigate reports of MDW abuse by employers or household members.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some MDWs were found in the course of Police investigations to have made false allegations against their employers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Police and MOM will not hesitate to take firm action against such MDWs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: She was also repatriated and banned from working in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We encourage employers and MDWs to maintain open communication with one another, discuss their concerns and resolve disputes amicably.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Fostering a sense of mutual trust and respect can help prevent misunderstandings from occurring.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MDWs are part of the caregiving solutions here.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MOM has introduced several measures to support MDW employers in hiring and managing their MDWs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will continue to find ways to safeguard the interests of MDW employers while protecting the well-being of MDWs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ultimately, for MDWs to continue to be part of the caregiving landscape, we strive to build a system that is fair to both the MDW employers and the MDWs.
